studies.title: The Gift Before The Insult
studies.meaning: Three lines and a complete argument. A gift is announced first, named by a word for something abundant that the surah does not define, and the commentators list many readings including a river in paradise. Then the response asked for is two acts, prayer and sacrifice, both of them things you give rather than things you keep. The last line answers an insult by reversing it, and nobody is named.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The sources report the occasion with reasonable agreement: the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had lost sons in infancy, and a Meccan opponent called him cut off, a man with no male line and therefore no future. The reports differ over who said it. The surah answers the taunt without repeating the name of the person who made it.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the root for muchness, so the word means abundance itself rather than a lot of something. It occurs only here, which is why the commentators list so many readings.
A specific verb for slaughtering a camel by a cut at the base of the neck, distinct from the word used for smaller animals. The instruction is concrete, and the meat from a camel feeds a crowd.
Used of an animal with a docked tail and of a man with no surviving sons. The surah takes the word the opponent used and hands it back, which is why the reply needs no argument.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's name survived through his sons and nowhere else. Genealogies were recited, and a line that ended was spoken of as cut. Losing infant sons was common and the grief was ordinary, but the social consequence was permanent: a man with daughters only was, in that reckoning, the last of his branch. The insult was not a cruelty invented for the occasion. It was a statement of fact as Mecca counted facts.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the shortest surah in the Quran, three ayat and about ten words in Arabic. The name of the man whose insult it answers is not in it. Neither is any argument. The reply is a single sentence that returns his own word to him. Its first line announces a gift in the past tense, before the insult is mentioned at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The surah answers a loss with a gift rather than with comfort, and the gift is announced in the past tense, as already given. That changes where the person addressed stands before the insult is even raised. What is asked in return is worship and slaughter, both outward and both costly. So the answer to abundance is not gratitude felt but something handed over. And the final reversal is stated without evidence, as a fact.

crossReferences.why: Answers a related accusation in the same period, that the one addressed had been left behind.
Pairs the same two acts, prayer and sacrifice, and extends them to a whole life.
Explains what is received from an offering, saying that neither meat nor blood reaches God but awareness does.

studies.applyIt: The next time someone says something belittling about your life, do not answer it. Instead write down one thing you have that you did not earn and could lose tomorrow. The surah replies to an insult by naming a gift, in that order, and the order is what makes the reply steady rather than defensive.
studies.explainEasier: God tells his messenger that he has given him a great deal. So he should pray to his Lord and offer a sacrifice. The man who hates him is the one who will end up with nothing.
